clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive demyelinating neuropathy whose defining histological hallmark is focal redundant myelin outfoldings on nerve biopsy, distinguishing it from most other demyelinating CMT.
Three allelic subtypes are recognised: CMT4B1 (MTMR2), CMT4B2 (SBF2/MTMR13) and CMT4B3 (SBF1/MTMR5), all converging on phosphoinositide 3-phosphatase regulation.
Onset is typically in early childhood with delayed motor milestones, distal weakness, foot deformity and a slowly ascending course to proximal muscles.
Motor nerve conduction velocities are markedly slowed in the demyelinating range, in keeping with a severe early-onset (Dejerine-Sottas-like) phenotype in many patients.
CMT4B2 characteristically associates with early-onset glaucoma, a clue that should prompt ophthalmological screening in a child with demyelinating neuropathy.
Bulbar and respiratory muscle involvement can occur in more severe cases, so monitoring of swallowing and respiratory function is warranted.
There is no disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive with orthotics, physiotherapy, foot surgery where indicated and avoidance of neurotoxic drugs.
reference.pathophysiology: CMT4B is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in genes encoding members of the myotubularin-related (MTMR) family of catalytically active and pseudophosphatase proteins: MTMR2 (CMT4B1), SBF2/MTMR13 (CMT4B2) and SBF1/MTMR5 (CMT4B3). MTMR2 is a phosphoinositide 3-phosphatase that dephosphorylates phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate and phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate, lipids that govern endosomal-lysosomal membrane trafficking and vesicle dynamics. SBF2 and SBF1 are catalytically dead pseudophosphatases that heterodimerise with and regulate the activity and localisation of active myotubularins. Loss of this phosphoinositide-regulating machinery in Schwann cells disrupts the tightly controlled membrane remodelling required to build and maintain compact myelin, producing the characteristic focal thickenings and redundant myelin outfoldings, segmental demyelination and secondary axonal loss that underlie the severe, early-onset demyelinating neuropathy.
additionalDifferentials: CMT4B1, CMT4B2 and CMT4B3 differentiated from one another (glaucoma points to CMT4B2)
Dejerine-Sottas disease (severe infantile demyelinating CMT of other genetic causes)
CMT1A and other dominant demyelinating CMT type 1 subtypes
CMT4C (SH3TC2) and other autosomal recessive demyelinating (CMT4) subtypes
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy presenting in childhood
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm a uniform demyelinating pattern with slowed conduction velocities
Targeted gene panel or exome sequencing covering MTMR2, SBF2 and SBF1
Sural nerve biopsy demonstrating myelin outfoldings and infoldings if genetic testing is inconclusive
Ophthalmological assessment including intraocular pressure measurement, especially where CMT4B2 is suspected
Respiratory function testing and swallowing assessment in severely affected children
Family segregation studies and carrier testing given autosomal recessive inheritance
redFlags: Progressive bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness requiring ventilatory support
New visual symptoms or raised intraocular pressure suggesting glaucoma in CMT4B2
Rapid deterioration out of keeping with a slowly progressive hereditary course, prompting reassessment for a superimposed acquired cause
Severe skeletal deformity compromising mobility or skin integrity
reference.prognosis: CMT4B is generally a severe, early-onset demyelinating neuropathy causing progressive disability and often loss of independent ambulation by adolescence or early adulthood, though the rate varies between subtypes and individuals. Life expectancy may be reduced when respiratory or bulbar involvement is prominent.
pitfalls: Mistaking the childhood demyelinating picture for an acquired inflammatory neuropathy and exposing the child to unnecessary immunotherapy
Overlooking the association of CMT4B2 with glaucoma and thereby missing preventable visual loss
Assuming dominant inheritance and failing to counsel unaffected carrier parents about recurrence risk
Attributing the phenotype to CMT1A without recognising the recessive pattern and the diagnostic myelin outfoldings on biopsy
references: International consensus guidance on inherited neuropathy classification
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Physiotherapy, orthoses and mobility aids for the early, often severe distal and ascending weakness
Ophthalmological screening with intraocular-pressure-lowering therapy for the early-onset glaucoma of the CMT4B2 subtype
Respiratory and swallowing surveillance with non-invasive ventilation and speech-and-language input in severely affected children
Orthopaedic management of foot deformity and scoliosis
Neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling with carrier testing and family screening
